reading_sub: A procedure that was signed, and a procedure that was followed
reading_title_html: The Alarm Nobody Stopped to Read

reading.rtitle: The Alarm Nobody Stopped to Read
paras: The general alarm on the main switchboard sounded at 0341 and continued for eleven minutes. The officer of the watch stopped monitoring it after the second minute, having decided that the malfunction was in the sensor rather than in the circuit. He did not stop to read the fault code, which would have taken about fifteen seconds and would have told him the opposite.

The company's own procedure is explicit. On any repeated alarm the watchkeeper is to record the code, notify the engine room and, if the alert persists beyond five minutes, wake the chief engineer. The pre-departure checklist covering that switchboard had been signed three days earlier. Investigators found no evidence that it had been worked through, and the officer, when asked, said he remembered signing it but did not remember checking anything.

The deviation that followed was small and expensive. With the alarm still sounding, the master elected to try running the affected section on the emergency generator, a step the contingency plan does not contain. It worked for forty minutes and then did not, and the vessel lost steering for a little over two minutes in a channel where two minutes is the whole margin.

The report is careful with its language. It notes that the officer regretted not reading the code, and that he had been on watch for eleven hours. It records that notification to the company was delayed by four hours and that the delay has not been explained. It concludes that the hazard was known, the procedure existed, the checklist had been signed, and none of those three facts had any effect whatever on what happened at 0341.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- engineering casualty report written for this lesson in the register of the PS-ASON reading passages

gist.prompt: What is the point the report is making?
choices: That the emergency generator was the wrong equipment for the job.
That the procedure, the checklist and the knowledge all existed and none of them changed what was done.
That the officer should have been relieved after eight hours on watch.

tf: The officer paused in order to read the fault code.
The text says he 'did not stop to read the fault code'. Stop to do means pause in order to do it -- and he did not.
The officer ceased watching the alarm two minutes after it began.
The text says he 'stopped monitoring it after the second minute'. Stop doing means cease the activity.
The officer recalled having signed the checklist.
The text says he 'remembered signing it but did not remember checking anything'.
Running the section on the emergency generator was a step foreseen in the contingency plan.
The text says it was 'a step the contingency plan does not contain'.
The company was informed without delay.
The text says 'notification to the company was delayed by four hours and the delay has not been explained'.

grammar_question: For each pair, say what actually happened and what did not. Then answer the one question the whole lesson turns on: which of the two forms describes an action that was COMPLETED?
grammar_rows: cease the activity / pause in order to do something else
He stopped monitoring it. / He stopped to read the code.
recall a past action / not forget a future obligation
He remembered signing it. / He must remember to sign it.
experiment with a method / attempt something difficult
He tried running it on the generator. / He tried to restart it.
be sorry about a past action / formal notification of bad news
He regretted not reading the code. / We regret to inform you.

the two forms are not stylistic variants: they describe DIFFERENT EVENTS. An option that swaps stopped monitoring for stopped to monitor reverses the fact while keeping every word of the sentence, and that is the cleanest distractor in the whole paper.
grammar_insight: In a procedure text these pairs are not grammar: they are the record of what was done. Read the second verb before you read the noun, because the second verb is the fact.

quickfire.situation: He stopped monitoring the alarm. Is he watching it now?
tips: No. Stop doing means the activity ended.
Stop to do would mean he paused in order to watch it.

quickfire.situation: He remembered signing the checklist. Did he sign it before or after remembering?
tips: Before. Remember doing looks back at a completed action.
Remember to do looks forward at an obligation.

quickfire.situation: Say the difference between he tried to restart it and he tried restarting it.
tips: Tried to restart: he attempted something difficult, maybe without success.
Tried restarting: he used restarting as a method to see whether it would help.

quickfire.situation: An option says: the officer stopped to read the fault code. Is that in the text?
tips: No, the opposite. The text says he did NOT stop to read it.
One word of difference and the fact reverses.

quickfire.situation: Say, in exam register, that nobody told the company for four hours.
tips: Notification to the company was delayed by four hours.
The company was not informed until four hours later.

quickfire.situation: We regret to inform you. Is the writer sorry about something already done, or announcing bad news?
tips: Announcing bad news. Regret to inform is a fixed formal opening.
Regret informing would mean he was sorry he had told you.

listenings.sub: The officer of the watch, interviewed six weeks later. Sound first -- no text.
listenings.text: I want to be accurate about this, because I have heard it repeated wrongly. I did not ignore the alarm. I watched it for two minutes, I decided it was the sensor, and then I stopped watching it. Those are two different things and only one of them is what I did. What I did not do, and what I regret, is stop to read the fault code. Fifteen seconds. The code would have told me the fault was in the circuit and I would have called the engine room at three forty-three instead of at four fifty. And yes, I had been on watch for eleven hours, and no, I am not offering that as an explanation. Plenty of people do eleven hours and read the code. I remember signing the checklist. I do not remember checking a single item on it, and I have said so from the first interview.
questions: What is the distinction he insists on at the start?
That he did not ignore the alarm. He watched it for two minutes, decided it was the sensor, and then stopped watching it -- which is a different thing.
What does he say he regrets, and how long would it have taken?
Not stopping to read the fault code. About fifteen seconds, and it would have told him the fault was in the circuit.
What does he say about the eleven hours and about the checklist?
He is not offering the eleven hours as an explanation. He remembers signing the checklist but does not remember checking a single item on it.

listenings.h: A Signature Is Not a Check
listenings.sub: A superintendent on why checklists stop working. Sound first -- no text.
listenings.text: Every checklist starts as a procedure and ends as a signature, and the interval is usually about two years. The first time a form is used, somebody walks the deck with it. The fiftieth time, somebody signs it in the office because he already knows what it says. And he does know. That is the uncomfortable part: the people who sign without checking are usually the ones who understand the system best. So we stopped adding items. Adding items is what everybody tries first, and it makes the problem worse, because the longer the form the faster it is signed. What we do now is change one item every month, without announcing which. If you have actually worked through the list, you notice. If you have remembered to sign it, you do not.
questions: What does she say happens to a checklist over about two years?
It starts as a procedure and ends as a signature. The first time somebody walks the deck with it; the fiftieth time somebody signs it in the office.
Why does she say adding items makes the problem worse?
Because the longer the form, the faster it is signed.
What do they do instead, and how does it reveal who really checked?
They change one item every month without announcing which. Whoever actually worked through the list notices; whoever only remembered to sign it does not.

pc_desc: The vocabulary of operational procedure and the four verb pairs where the form changes the fact. Key words: procedure, malfunction, alert, deviation, contingency, drill, hazard, checklist, precaution, notification. Structure: gerund and infinitive with a change of meaning.

paras: The officer stopped monitoring the alarm after the second minute. He did not stop to read the fault code, which would have taken about fifteen seconds and would have told him the opposite.

He said that he remembered signing the checklist but did not remember checking anything. The master elected to try running the affected section on the emergency generator, a step the contingency plan does not contain. The report notes that the officer regretted not reading the code, and closes with the sentence every company dreads: we regret to inform you.

quiz.q: He stopped monitoring the alarm. Was he still watching it afterwards?
opts: Yes. He paused and then continued.
No. Stop + -ing means the activity ended.
The sentence does not say.

quiz.q: He remembered signing the checklist. When did the signing happen?
opts: Before the remembering. The action is already complete.
After the remembering. It was an obligation he fulfilled.
At the same moment.

quiz.q: The master elected to try running the section on the generator. What does try + -ing tell you?
opts: That it was very difficult and he may have failed.
That running it on the generator was a method he used to see whether it would help.
That he refused to do it.

grammar_tip_title: Gerund or Infinitive -- When the Form Is the Fact
grammar_tip_lead: Most verbs take one form or the other and nothing changes. Four of them change the EVENT, and all four appear in procedure writing. Read the second verb first: it is where the fact lives.

teacher.s1: Abertura (2 min): DECISAO DE DESENHO do programa: toda aula e reading-driven, sem alternar com aula de fala (a REGRA 29.2 nao se aplica aqui), porque a prova e 100% leitura. Entre direto, sem cumprimento scriptado (REGRA 27A).
teacher.s2: Homework check + warm-up (5 min): Ela sublinhou oracoes relativas num paragrafo real da IMO. Peca duas e o CRITERIO que ela usou. Se o criterio for 'porque faz sentido', volte trinta segundos ao slide 3 da aula 6 -- e o mesmo defeito.
teacher.s3: Provocacao (5 min): As duas frases tem as mesmas palavras. Espere ela separar. Se travar, pergunte: after the sentence, is he looking at the alarm or not? A segunda pergunta (qual delas um relatorio prefere escrever) e a que importa: o relatorio escreve a que descreve o que NAO foi feito.
teacher.s4: Objetivo (2 min): Diga: the words of a procedure, four verb pairs, and what the wrong form does to an operation.
teacher.s5: Transicao vocab (1 min): Diga: Ten words that only exist because something can go wrong. Passe ao proximo.
teacher.s6: Vocab reveal 1-4 (5 min): procedure, malfunction, alert, deviation. NAO traduza (REGRA 13). CCQ para deviation: Is a deviation always a mistake? (Nao -- e um afastamento do planejado, e pode ser deliberado e correto.) CCQ para alert: Is an alert the same as an alarm? (Proximo, mas alert e a NOTIFICACAO formal.)
teacher.s7: Vocab reveal 5-7 (5 min): contingency, drill, hazard. CCQ para hazard: Does a hazard mean something has gone wrong? (NAO -- hazard existe ANTES; e a fonte de perigo. Contraste com incident.) Ela ja viu drill na aula 5 dentro de lifeboat drill: aqui e a palavra sozinha.
teacher.s8: Vocab reveal 8-10 (5 min): checklist, precaution, notification. CCQ para precaution: Is a precaution taken before or after? (Antes -- e a diferenca com corrective action, que vem na aula 9.) O listening 2 e inteiro sobre checklist: avise que ela vai ouvir a palavra viva.
teacher.s9: Consolidate (4 min): Ela toca a palavra e le a definicao em voz alta antes de fechar o par.
teacher.s10: Transicao leitura (1 min): Diga: Everything on this ship existed. None of it worked. O proximo slide e o de TAREFA: a pergunta ANTES do texto.
teacher.s11: Leitura (7 min): Tres minutos em silencio, sem dicionario. NAO traduza. Avise UMA vez, antes de comecar: neste texto o verbo depois do verbo decide o fato. Depois UMA frase de resumo.
teacher.s12: Gist (3 min): Ela escolhe e JUSTIFICA. As opcoes (a) e (c) sao verdadeiras no texto e nao sao o PONTO -- e a armadilha de gist mais comum da prova.
teacher.s13: True or False (7 min): REGRA DA CASA: TRUE ou FALSE e DEPOIS a linha que prova. As afirmacoes 1 e 2 sao o par stop to do / stop doing, e sao a aula inteira.
teacher.s14: Transicao gramatica (1 min): Diga: Now the four pairs. Passe ao proximo.
teacher.s15: Grammar discovery (7 min): Nao de a regra. Para cada exemplo pergunte: what happened, and what did not? So entao clique Reveal the Rule. CCQ decisivo: 'He remembered signing it' -- did he sign it? (Sim.) 'He must remember to sign it' -- has he signed it? (Ainda nao.) Ela estuda gramatica sozinha: aqui e ferramenta de leitura, nao producao.
teacher.s16: Practice (4 min): Ela diz a forma ORALMENTE antes de clicar.
teacher.s17: Spot the error (4 min): Atencao: aqui as quatro frases erradas sao GRAMATICALMENTE CORRETAS -- o erro e de SENTIDO contra o texto. Diga isso a ela antes, senao o exercicio parece quebrado.
teacher.s18: Transicao equivalencia (1 min): Diga: Same eleven minutes, other words. Passe ao proximo.
teacher.s19: Como a prova esconde (4 min): O terceiro par (stopped monitoring -> ceased to observe) e o que mais engana: 'ceased to observe' TEM infinitivo e mesmo assim significa parar de fazer. Explique que ceased to do e stopped doing sao equivalentes, e que stop e a excecao.
teacher.s20: Equivalencia (5 min): Depois de fechar os pares, cubra a direita e faca a direcao dificil.
teacher.s21: Complete (5 min): Teacher-led, uma lacuna por vez. As oito respostas sao oito das dez palavras da aula.
teacher.s22: Quick fire (6 min): Uma por vez, em voz alta, antes das dicas. A quarta e a que reproduz o distrator real da prova.
teacher.s23: Transicao (1 min): Diga: The officer himself, and then somebody who has thought about why checklists die. Passe ao proximo.
teacher.s24: Listening 1 (5 min): LEIA AS 3 PERGUNTAS EM VOZ ALTA COM ELA ANTES de tocar (REGRA 2.1). Escuta medida em 0%: 0.75x na primeira vez. Este audio usa TRES dos quatro pares. Peca que ela identifique os tres na segunda escuta.
teacher.s25: Listening 2 (5 min): LEIA AS 3 PERGUNTAS EM VOZ ALTA COM ELA ANTES de tocar (REGRA 2.1). A ultima frase do audio ('If you have remembered to sign it, you do not') e o par remember to do usado com precisao cirurgica. Volte a ela.
teacher.s26: Role-play guiado (4 min): Cinco frases com os frames. Conte quantos pares corretos ela produz.
teacher.s27: Role-play semi-livre (5 min): Este e o exercicio central da aula: dizer o que a OUTRA forma significaria e o que teria de ser diferente a bordo. Nao aceite so a traducao do sentido -- exija a consequencia operacional.
teacher.s28: Producao livre (6 min): Nao interrompa. Mede-se: tres pares corretos e a palavra precaution usada ao menos uma vez.
teacher.s29: Transicao wrap-up (1 min): Diga: Let us see what you can do now.
teacher.s30: Survival card (3 min): Cinco frases do proprio texto. Insista no ritmo: 'stopped MOnitoring' x 'stopped to READ' -- a acentuacao ajuda a fixar a diferenca.
teacher.s31: Checklist (2 min): Leia cada item em voz alta. Os 5 checks fecham a aula e acendem o stamp.
teacher.s32: Encerramento (2 min): Diga: Lesson 7 complete, Helena. HOMEWORK ORALMENTE, nunca escrito na tela: (1) escrever oito pares de frases -- a mesma situacao nas duas formas -- e dizer, em uma linha, o que muda a bordo em cada par; (2) achar num texto tecnico real em ingles tres ocorrencias de stop, remember, try ou regret e classificar cada uma.
